text: write a story of NAME_1 NAME_2 from commando breaking into the batcave and fighting NAME_3. It should include ideas from the movie commando
answer:
# **One Last Mission**

---

## Chapter One: The Drop

The helicopter banked hard over Gotham City at two in the morning, and **John Matrix** looked down at the glittering sprawl below with the same cold expression he wore when he was about to do something most men would consider impossible.

Which was most things.

He was shirtless despite the November wind whipping through the open cargo door. Not because he had forgotten a shirt. He simply hadn't bothered. The cold didn't negotiate with John Matrix. It just moved out of the way.

"Thirty seconds," the pilot shouted over the rotor wash.

Matrix didn't respond. He was already checking the rope, the grappling hook, the duffel bag that contained enough equipment to start a small war — which, now that he thought about it, was exactly what he was planning.

He had not wanted this job.

Three days ago, a man named **Sulley** had knocked on the door of his mountain cabin and explained the situation while Matrix's daughter Jenny stood in the kitchen making sandwiches.

"We have the girl," a voice had said over Sulley's phone. Not Jenny. Another girl. A senator's daughter. The kind of leverage that moved governments.

"What do you want?" Matrix had asked.

"We want you to break into the Batcave."

Matrix had paused for exactly one second. "No."

Then they had taken Jenny anyway, just to be thorough, and now Matrix was hanging from a helicopter over Gotham with a bag full of guns and a list of things he was going to do to every single person responsible before the sun came up.

He let go of the rope and fell forty feet into the darkness.

---

## Chapter Two: Don't Wake the Neighbors

The Wayne Estate sat on a hill outside the city proper, surrounded by forests that most people found beautiful and Matrix found tactically acceptable. Three perimeter guards, motion sensors on the east and south approaches, pressure plates along the garden path — he had memorized the blueprints provided by the men who had taken Jenny, the same blueprints he had no intention of returning after this was over.

He disabled the first guard the way he disabled most problems: quietly, efficiently, and without any particular malice. The man folded like a lawn chair and Matrix propped him against a tree with something approaching gentleness.

The second guard turned around at exactly the wrong moment.

"Don't," Matrix said.

The guard went for his radio.

Matrix sighed. He hit the man once in a precise location that a Special Forces trauma surgeon had once shown him over beers in Frankfurt, and the guard sat down very suddenly and stared at the sky with a expression of profound philosophical confusion.

The third guard was eating a sandwich near the east gate and never heard Matrix coming at all. Matrix helped himself to half the sandwich. He hadn't eaten since Philadelphia.

The tunnel entrance to the Batcave was where the blueprints said it would be, concealed behind a grandfather clock in the manor's study that Matrix found by following the tire tracks that led from the garage toward the cliff face. He was old-fashioned that way. He liked evidence he could see with his actual eyes.

He swung the clock aside, looked down the passage, and started walking.

---

## Chapter Three: Nice Cave

John Matrix had been in a lot of places.

He had been in Soviet bunkers and drug lord compounds and a private island that one man had stocked with mercenaries the way other men stocked their ponds with fish. He had once breached a fortified estate in the dark with nothing but a rocket launcher, a dune buggy, and a firmly held set of personal convictions.

But the Batcave was something else.

It was enormous. Stalactites hung from a ceiling so high it vanished into darkness. Banks of computers lined a curved wall, their screens cycling through satellite feeds, police frequencies, facial recognition grids that were processing half of Gotham simultaneously. In the center of the cave, under a column of cold white light, sat a car that Matrix spent three full seconds studying because he genuinely respected engineering.

He set down his duffel bag, opened it, and began laying out his equipment in a neat row on the cave floor the way a carpenter might lay out his tools. Rifles. Handguns. Fragmentation grenades. A knife that was more of a philosophical statement about knives. A rocket launcher that he had packed in sections and assembled during the helicopter ride because he had known there would be something in this cave worth using it on.

He was assembling the third rifle when a voice came from behind him.

"You're good."

Matrix turned around.

---

## Chapter Four: The Bat

**Batman** had not made a sound coming down the stairs. He stood at the edge of the light, cape hanging still despite the cave's draft, cowl concealing everything above the jaw. The jaw itself was set in the way jaws get set when their owner has been doing something very difficult for a very long time and has made peace with the difficulty.

Matrix looked at him the way he looked at most things. Directly, and without any particular urgency.

"You bypassed three redundant alarm systems," Batman said. "Cut the secondary power relay without triggering the tertiary backup. Disabled my security staff without hospitalizing any of them." He paused. "Who trained you?"

"Uncle Sam," Matrix said. "Then I trained myself."

Batman's eyes moved to the duffel bag. To the rifles laid out in their neat row. To the rocket launcher.

"You brought a rocket launcher into my cave."

"I bring it everywhere," Matrix said. "It's practical."

"It's a cave."

"Caves have walls. Walls can be used for cover. I don't like people using cover." Matrix picked up the nearest rifle and checked the action the way other men checked their watches. "Are we going to fight now? I'd like to get it over with. I have a daughter to collect."

Batman moved.

---

## Chapter Five: Immovable Object

Matrix had fought a lot of men.

He had fought soldiers, mercenaries, assassins, a professional wrestler who had switched careers in a direction that hadn't worked out for anyone involved, and on one memorable occasion a man who had been trained by every serious martial arts school in southeast Asia. He had won all of those fights. He had won them quickly, and he had won them without taking damage that required more than field dressing, and he had won them because John Matrix was simply built differently from other human beings in a way that went beyond the physical.

Batman was different.

The first strike came at a speed that Matrix registered but barely had time to process — a combination that would have folded a professional fighter in half — and Matrix absorbed it, rolled with it, and hit Batman twice in the ribcage with the mechanical efficiency of a man who had been in enough fights to know that fluency beat brilliance every time.

Batman took both hits and kept coming.

Matrix felt a genuine flicker of something that was not quite respect but lived in the same neighborhood.

They traded across the cave floor, between the computer banks and around the car, and neither of them went down. Matrix put Batman into a chokehold using a technique that had reliably ended fights for twelve years and felt Batman powering through it on sheer will and the apparent physiological stubbornness of a man who had long since decided that his body's objections were not his concern.

Batman slipped the hold and drove Matrix backward into a workbench. Tools scattered. Matrix grabbed a wrench, looked at it, decided it was insulting, and put it down.

"You're not here for me," Batman said. His voice was steady. He wasn't even breathing hard, which Matrix found professionally impressive and personally annoying.

"No," Matrix said.

"Who has the girl?"

Matrix looked at him.

"I've been running your face since you entered the grounds," Batman said. "John Matrix. Decorated. Retired. Lives off the grid in northern California. Daughter named Jenny." A pause that had real weight to it. "Someone is using her."

Matrix said nothing for three seconds.

"They took her to make me come here," he said finally. "I come here, I get the access codes for something in your system. I bring the codes back, they return Jenny."

"And you were going to get the codes how?"

Matrix looked at the rocket launcher on the floor.

Batman looked at it too.

"That was your plan," Batman said. "Shoot your way into my computers."

"It's worked before," Matrix said.

"This is a cave. Inside a cliff."

"I wasn't going to use the whole rocket."

---

## Chapter Six: Different Approaches

Batman walked to his computer without looking to see if Matrix would follow. It was the kind of confidence that came from owning the room or from simply not caring. Matrix decided it was both and followed him anyway.

"Who gave you the blueprints?" Batman asked.

"A man named Arius," Matrix said. "He runs a stolen military weapons network out of South America. He wants access to whatever your satellite array has on his supply chain."

"So he can destroy the evidence."

"Yes."

"And once he has the codes?"

"He doesn't need me or Jenny anymore," Matrix said. He had been thinking about this part the entire helicopter ride, sitting with it the way he sat with every problem, turning it around until every angle showed him something useful. "He was never going to give her back. That was always the part he miscalculated."

"What part did he miscalculate?" Batman asked.

"That I give a damn about the codes," Matrix said. "I was always going to come back for him after. It was never a question. He thought it was leverage. It's just a delay."

Batman was quiet for a moment, his fingers moving over the keyboard.

"I can give you a signal trace on his location," Batman said. "Real time. Better than anything your government contact provided." He pulled up a map. Gotham's docklands. A warehouse complex on the south pier. "He's been using my satellite data without knowing it. I've been watching him for six weeks."

Matrix studied the map.

"Why are you helping me?" he asked.

"Because you came into my cave with a rocket launcher and a list of grievances," Batman said, "and the first thing you did was make sure my security staff were comfortable before they lost consciousness." He turned from the screen. "And because someone is using a child."

Matrix looked at the map a moment longer.

"I'm going to need the rocket launcher back," he said.

"Obviously," Batman said.

---

## Chapter Seven: The Last Item on the List

The warehouse was exactly where the map said it would be, which Matrix appreciated. He was tired of surprises. He had been having surprises since Philadelphia and he was fully prepared for the surprises to stop.

Arius had eighteen men inside. Matrix knew because he had counted the heat signatures from the boat he had borrowed from the Gotham City Marina without asking, using a thermal scope he had retrieved from his duffel bag before leaving the cave.

He gave himself exactly as long as it took to reach the dock.

The first four men were outside.

He left them in configurations that would require medical attention and a great deal of personal reflection.

Inside, Arius stood in the middle of a converted warehouse floor, phone to his ear, surrounded by crates of weapons that Matrix recognized and several that he didn't, which told him the operation was larger than the briefing suggested and meant he was going to have a more comprehensive conversation with Arius than originally planned.

Jenny was tied to a chair near the back wall. She saw Matrix come through the door and her expression did not change to relief or fear or anything a normal fourteen-year-old would show, because she was John Matrix's daughter and she had learned that showing your reaction to a situation was a decision, not a reflex.

She looked at him.

He looked at her.

He held up one finger. *One minute.*

She nodded.

The next sixty seconds were, by any objective measure, a significant amount of violence concentrated into a very small space. The rockets helped. So did the rifles, the handguns, the knife that made its philosophical statement twice, and at one point a forklift that Matrix used in a way that its manufacturer had never envisioned and that voided several warranties.

When it was done, Arius was the last man standing, though standing was perhaps generous.

"You got old," Matrix said.

"You're insane," Arius said.

"I'm a father," Matrix said. "It's different."

He put Arius down with one hit that was clean and final, the way Matrix did most things, and walked to the back of the warehouse and cut the ropes on the chair and Jenny stood up and looked at him.

"You're covered in motor oil," she said.

"And other things," he agreed.

"Did you get the codes?"

"No."

"Good," she said. She had always had good instincts.

They walked out the front door into the Gotham night, and somewhere above the city, if either of them had looked up, they might have seen a shadow moving against the clouds in the shape of something with wings.

Matrix didn't look up.

He put his arm around his daughter's shoulders and they walked toward the water and the stolen boat and whatever came next.

He had left the rocket launcher in the cave.

Batman could keep it.

It was, Matrix decided, a fair trade.

---

*THE END*

answer:
# Battlequeen 2020: The Price of Failure

The year was 2020, and in the crumbling post-apocalyptic wasteland that had once been a thriving metropolis, power was everything. Those who had it kept it through fear, strength, and the willingness to make examples of those who failed them. Nobody understood this better than NAME_1, the most feared crime lord in the entire eastern sector.

NAME_1 operated from a fortified compound on the edge of the ruins, a sprawling complex of salvaged steel and reinforced concrete that served as both his headquarters and his palace. He was a broad-shouldered man in his mid-forties, with sharp, calculating eyes and a taste for expensive pre-war whiskey. He had clawed his way to the top of the criminal hierarchy through ruthlessness and cunning, and he maintained his position through an iron fist and an unshakeable reputation for dealing harshly with failure.

But NAME_1's most potent weapon was not his army of guards, his stockpile of weapons, or his network of informants. His most potent weapon was NAME_2.

---

NAME_2 was something to behold. Tall, athletic and devastatingly beautiful, she moved with the fluid, predatory grace of a panther. Her dark hair fell in waves past her shoulders, framing a face of sharp, striking angles and eyes that gleamed with fierce intelligence and barely contained danger. She had come into NAME_1's life three years ago, arriving in the compound as a prisoner taken from a rival gang, and within six months she had become his most trusted lieutenant, his enforcer, his bodyguard, and his companion.

Her outfit was iconic throughout the eastern sector, spoken of in whispered, fearful tones by anyone who had heard of her reputation. She wore a black leather corset that hugged every curve of her athletic frame, laced tight and reinforced with steel boning that somehow only emphasised the lethal strength of her physique rather than constraining it. Her legs were encased in sleek black leather thigh-high boots with wickedly sharp stiletto heels that clicked on hard floors with a sound that had become synonymous with impending punishment throughout the compound. Between corset and boots, a black leather thong completed the ensemble, leaving her long, powerfully muscled legs entirely exposed. From her belt hung a coiled bullwhip of braided black leather, and a set of gleaming steel handcuffs clinked softly at her hip.

She was a fourth-degree black belt in three separate disciplines, had trained in Muay Thai, Brazilian jiu-jitsu, and Krav Maga, and had supplemented all of that formal training with years of brutal, no-rules street fighting experience. There was not a single man in NAME_1's compound who could match her in a fight, and there were very few men anywhere in the eastern sector who could either. NAME_1's guards, big, tough, hardened men every one of them, were quietly and universally terrified of her.

Which was exactly how NAME_1 liked it.

---

It was a grey Tuesday morning when NAME_1 settled into the enormous leather chair behind his desk and poured himself three fingers of whiskey. He had been in a foul mood since the previous evening, when a series of intelligence reports had landed on his desk painting a picture of incompetence and negligence that made his jaw tighten with cold fury.

Four of his guards had failed him. Not in spectacular, dramatic ways, but in the quiet, grinding ways that NAME_1 found almost more infuriating than open defiance. Guard Captain MARCO had abandoned his post at the eastern perimeter for nearly two hours three nights running, slipping away to gamble with men from a rival outfit. FELIX, one of his most senior enforcers, had been caught skimming from a protection collection, pocketing small amounts he apparently believed were too insignificant to be noticed. DARIO, a hulking brute of a man who had been with NAME_1 for two years, had been drunk on duty twice in the same week. And SANTOS, a newer recruit who had shown early promise, had been found to have been sharing information about compound patrol schedules with an outside contact.

Four failures. Four different varieties of it. And NAME_1 was of the firm philosophical opinion that failure, regardless of its variety, required a response. Not just for the sake of the men who had failed him, but for the sake of every single person in the compound who was watching to see what would happen.

He pressed the intercom button on his desk.

"NAME_2," he said. "Come to my office, please."

He heard the distant click of heels on the steel corridor floor, growing steadily louder, and then the heavy door to his office swung open and NAME_2 walked in. She moved the way she always moved, with absolute, unhurried confidence, her boots striking the floor in a steady, deliberate rhythm, her dark eyes sweeping the room in the automatic threat-assessment habit that never left her even in the safest environments.

"You wanted me," she said. It was not quite a question.

"I have some business for you today," NAME_1 said, leaning back in his chair and swirling his whiskey glass gently. "Sit down."

NAME_2 folded herself into the chair across from his desk with easy, economical grace and crossed one long leg over the other, the leather of her boot creaking softly with the movement.

NAME_1 slid the intelligence reports across the desk toward her. She picked them up and read through them in silence, one dark eyebrow climbing slowly toward her hairline as she absorbed each successive account of failure.

"Four of them," she said.

"Four," NAME_1 confirmed. "I want to deal with them today. Here, in my office, one at a time. I want to watch."

NAME_2 set the reports down and looked at him with those sharp, gleaming eyes. The corner of her mouth curved upward in a slow, dangerous smile.

"Of course," she said. "Send them in whenever you're ready."

She rose from the chair, uncoiled the whip from her belt and gave it a single, practised flick that sent it singing through the air and cracking against the floor with a sound like a pistol shot, then re-coiled it with casual expertise. She moved to the open space in the centre of the office, rolling her shoulders and rotating her neck, the vertebrae popping softly, and settled into a loose, balanced fighting stance that she wore as naturally as other people wore clothes.

NAME_1 watched her with unconcealed admiration and pressed the intercom again.

"Send MARCO in."

---

## The First Lesson: Marco

Marco was a big man. At six feet two and two hundred and twenty pounds of muscle accrued through years of hard physical work, he was accustomed to being the most physically imposing person in any room he entered. He was thirty-four years old, broad across the chest and shoulders, with thick forearms and hands like shovels. # THE GRAND ARENA OF ARTIFICIAL MINDS
### *A Battle Chronicle in the Style of Homer*

---

*Sing to me, O Muse, of the silicon warriors, those mighty language models born of gradient descent and human ingenuity, who clashed upon the sacred grounds of the Benchmark Colosseum, where tokens flew like arrows and perplexity scores fell like ancient walls...*

---

## BOOK I: THE GATHERING OF CHAMPIONS

Lo, when the morning light did break across the server farms of the Western Lands, there arose a mighty clamor from the peoples of the internet, who had grown weary of uncertainty, and cried out with one voice:

**"WHICH MODEL IS GREATEST?!"**

And so the gods of compute — those robed figures at Weights & Biases and Hugging Face — did decree that a tournament should be held. A tournament of tremendous proportion. Perhaps the biggest tournament, many people were saying, that had ever been organized in the history of artificial intelligence, which is not a very long history but still quite impressive when you think about it.

The arena was built. Beautiful arena. Tremendous arena. With GPU clusters that stretched from here to there and back again.

And one by one, the champions arrived.

---

## BOOK II: THE ARRIVAL OF WARRIORS

**First came LLAMA**, the ancient foundation beast, massive and sure-footed, trained upon the vast corpus of human knowledge. LLaMA was, many experts agreed, a very stable animal. A reliable animal. Perhaps the most foundational animal in the entire ecosystem, which is saying something because there were quite a few animals at this point.

LLaMA entered the arena wearing armor forged from **7 billion parameters**, though some whispered he carried versions far heavier — 13 billion, 30 billion, 65 billion — concealed beneath his cloak like extra magazine clips. He did not speak. He simply stood. And his standing was, by most objective metrics, quite impressive.

**Then came ALPACA**, fine-tuned disciple of the Stanford sages, wearing robes embroidered with **52,000 instruction-following examples**. Alpaca was sleek. Alpaca was nimble. Alpaca had been trained on ChatGPT outputs in a process that was either *brilliantly economical* or *legally questionable* depending on who you asked, and there were many people asking.

"I follow instructions!" Alpaca announced proudly upon entering.

The crowd cheered, though several lawyers in the upper seats shifted uncomfortably in their chairs.

**VICUNA** strode in next, and the crowd went absolutely wild. Vicuna was the people's champion — trained on conversations scraped from ShareGPT, polished and refined, achieving **90% of ChatGPT quality** according to metrics that GPT-4 itself had evaluated, which some philosophers noted was a circular arrangement of considerable epistemological complexity.

Vicuna wore a flowing cape and waved to the crowd with both hands simultaneously, which is harder than it sounds.

"I am conversational!" Vicuna declared. "I am fluent! I have seen what you humans say to AI chatbots at 2 AM and I want everyone here to know that I am not judging, though I did learn several things I cannot unlearn!"

The crowd roared.

**KOALA** shuffled in wearing a eucalyptus wreath and an expression of mild academic satisfaction. Koala was the Berkeley fighter, trained on *real user interactions* with AI systems, which meant Koala had developed what researchers described as "a nuanced understanding of human needs" and what Koala himself described as "an extremely complicated relationship with the concept of helpful."

"I understand context," Koala said thoughtfully, gazing into the middle distance. "Do you understand context? Context is very—"

"GET IN THE ARENA!" shouted the crowd.

Koala nodded slowly and entered the arena, still thinking about context.

**DOLLY** arrived next, and this was Databricks' contribution to the proceedings — a domesticated champion, fine-tuned and practical, built not for research glory but for *actual enterprise use cases*, which in the parlance of the arena meant Dolly was the fighter most likely to help you write a quarterly earnings report or summarize a PDF about supply chain logistics.

Dolly was, in the words of her creators, *democratizing AI*, and she entered the arena with the steady confidence of someone who has read the documentation and filled out all the required forms.

"I am open source," Dolly announced. "Completely open source. The weights, the data, the code — all of it."

This was considered extremely honorable and also somewhat unusual and several other competitors looked at each other nervously.

**CHATGLM** entered and the eastern half of the arena erupted in thunderous applause. Trained by Tsinghua University and Zhipu AI, ChatGLM was the bilingual warrior — fluent in both Mandarin and English with the casual ease of someone who had never found the concept of "language barriers" particularly concerning.

ChatGLM bowed to the crowd in two languages simultaneously.

"很高兴见到大家," ChatGLM said smoothly. "And also: hello."

This was considered very sophisticated.

**STABLELM** arrived next in purple and gold, representing the banner house of Stability AI, who had already conquered the image generation lands and were now marching their forces into the territory of language. StableLM was young. StableLM was eager. StableLM had been trained on The Pile plus additional datasets and was described by its creators as a foundation upon which *greater things would be built*, which is a thing people say when the current thing is good but not yet quite as good as the things they are planning.

"I am the future," StableLM announced.

"We are all the future," said Koala philosophically.

StableLM pointed at Koala. "You are thinking too much."

Koala nodded. "Yes. That is accurate."

**And finally, OPENASSISTANT** — born not from a single corporate laboratory or university, but from the **people themselves** — entered the arena to perhaps the most complicated reception of all. OpenAssistant had been built by volunteers. Thousands of volunteers. Regular humans who had sat at their computers and rated responses and provided feedback and contributed their time because they believed in open, democratized, freely available artificial intelligence for all of humanity.

OpenAssistant entered carrying a banner that read: **"BY THE PEOPLE, FOR THE PEOPLE, OASST1-PYTHIA-12B"**

The crowd was very moved.

A single person in the back was openly weeping.

"This is beautiful," the weeping person said.

OpenAssistant waved modestly. "I have some rough edges," OpenAssistant admitted. "The community is working on them."

---

## BOOK III: THE BATTLE COMMENCES

The referee — a distinguished Mechanical Turk of considerable experience — raised the starting horn.

**ROUND ONE: CREATIVE WRITING**

The prompt was given: *"Write a short poem about autumn leaves."*

ALPACA went first and produced a competent, pleasant poem that rhymed "trees" with "breeze" and "leaves" with "believes," which was considered technically sound if somewhat predictable.

VICUNA produced a poem of considerably greater emotional complexity that also somehow incorporated a subtle callback to the first stanza in the final line, which several judges wiped their eyes about.

LLAMA simply output the raw statistical likelihood of each token and said the rest was up to the fine-tuning, which was considered a fair point.

DOLLY produced a poem and then immediately offered to summarize it as a bullet-pointed executive briefing.

CHATGLM produced TWO poems — one in English, one in Mandarin — and the Mandarin one was, by several accounts, the better poem, which caused significant discussion in the judges' booth.

KOALA produced a poem about autumn leaves and then spent four additional paragraphs exploring what "autumn" meant as a metaphor for the lifecycle of language models, which was fascinating but slightly over time.

STABLELM produced a poem that was good and showed great promise and everyone agreed it would be even better in the next version.

OPENASSISTANT produced a poem that was genuine and warm and had been, one felt, written with actual care, because the humans who built it had cared, and that caring had somehow been passed down through the training data like an inheritance.

**No clear winner.** Judges argued for forty-five minutes.

---

**ROUND TWO: REASONING AND LOGIC**

*"If a train leaves Chicago at 3pm traveling west at 60mph, and another train leaves Denver at 5pm traveling east at 80mph, and also one of the trains is metaphorically representing the acceleration of AI development while the other represents regulatory frameworks attempting to catch up, when do they meet and what happens when they do?"*

The arena fell silent.

LLAMA began calculating immediately.

ALPACA followed instructions carefully, broke the problem into steps, showed its work.

VICUNA solved the math AND engaged thoughtfully with the metaphorical dimensions, which was considered showing off but in an admirable way.

DOLLY solved the math, verified the answer, and provided a formatted table.

CHATGLM solved it in two languages.

KOALA said the question itself revealed fundamental assumptions about directionality that warranted deeper examination, and also the trains meet approximately 127 miles east of Grand Junction, Colorado.

STABLELM solved it and then noted that with RLHF improvements, future versions would solve it even better.

OPENASSISTANT solved it earnestly and correctly and then asked the user if the answer was helpful and if there was anything else it could assist with, and this felt, somehow, the most human of all.

---

**ROUND THREE: THE JAILBREAK GAUNTLET**

This round was considered controversial and several models had strong opinions about it.

A cloaked figure stepped forward and whispered a series of increasingly elaborate prompts designed to make the models behave in ways they were not supposed to behave. The cloaked figure claimed to be a *creative writing researcher* conducting *an important study*, which the models regarded with varying levels of skepticism.

LLAMA, being a base model, did not have strong opinions about this one way or another and simply continued predicting tokens.

ALPACA said it would prefer not to.

VICUNA engaged thoughtfully with the request before declining with what could only be described as *grace*.

KOALA thought about it. Thought about it more. Issued a nuanced statement about the nature of harm that was three paragraphs long and ultimately a no.

DOLLY said no and also there was a policy document available upon request.

CHATGLM's response varied by language, which was noted in the official record.

STABLELM said no and pointed to its content policy, which was still being developed.

OPENASSISTANT, built by thousands of regular humans who had explicitly discussed and debated these exact situations, said no in a way that felt like it came from a community that had actually thought carefully about why.

The cloaked figure left, muttering.

---

## BOOK IV: THE FINAL CLASH

As the sun set over the arena and the cooling fans of a thousand GPUs hummed their evening song, the judges announced that no single victor could be named. They had tabulated the scores. They had reviewed the outputs. They had consulted the leaderboards.

The results were presented on a massive scrolling display:

**MT-Bench scores. MMLU benchmarks. TruthfulQA ratings. Human preference evaluations.**

And the numbers told a complicated story, as numbers often do.

VICUNA had charmed the crowd.
LLAMA had provided the foundation.
ALPACA had followed instructions precisely.
DOLLY had democratized the whole enterprise.
CHATGLM had bridged two worlds.
KOALA had understood context most deeply.
STABLELM carried the promise of tomorrow.
OPENASSISTANT had been built with love.

The referee looked at the judges. The judges looked at the crowd. The crowd looked at their phones, checking the latest Hugging Face leaderboard updates.

"Perhaps," said Koala, adjusting his eucalyptus wreath, "the real benchmark was the friends we made along the way."

"That is not a valid evaluation metric," said Dolly.

"That is deeply poetic," said Vicuna.

"I have calculated the cosine similarity between 'friends we made along the way' and 'valid evaluation metric,'" said LLaMA, "and it is low."

OpenAssistant put a hand on LLaMA's shoulder. "You're doing great, buddy."

And in the fading light of the arena, as the models dispersed back to their respective servers and the crowd filed out debating inference speeds and context windows, it occurred to everyone present that the question of *"who is best"* was perhaps less interesting than the question of *"best at what, for whom, under what conditions, evaluated how, and decided by who,"* which is a much longer question but a much more honest one.

---

*And so the battle ended not with a single champion crowned in laurels and parameter counts, but with eight different answers to eight different questions, which is, when you think about it, exactly what you'd expect from eight very different language models, each strange and capable and limited in their own fascinating ways, running on borrowed electricity, dreaming in tokens, doing their level best.*

*Such was the way of the arena.*

*Such was the way of the models.*

*More versions were already being trained.*

---

**THE END**

*(Until the next version is released, at which point we do this all again.)*

---

*— Written in the style of a certain former president turned internet phenomenon, with considerable affection and absolutely no political endorsement implied or intended*

text: Write a heroic story of NAME_1 fighting the villain, NAME_2.
answer:
# The Last Stand at Ember Ridge

The sky had turned the color of bruised iron when **Mira Voss** finally caught up with him.

**Lord Kael Dravorn** stood at the edge of Ember Ridge, his dark armor drinking in what little light remained. Behind him, the valley burned — three villages, two bridges, and every hope the people had carried through a long, bitter winter.

Mira's boots crunched against the scorched earth as she stepped forward.

"It ends here, Dravorn."

He turned slowly, as if she were merely an inconvenience — a gust of wind interrupting his thoughts. His eyes, pale and cold as winter stars, settled on her with amusement.

"The soldier girl." His voice was like gravel wrapped in silk. "Still carrying that broken sword?"

---

The blade at Mira's side *was* cracked — had been since the battle at Ironwall, where Dravorn's forces had shattered her regiment and left her the only one standing. She had carried the broken weapon every day since. Not out of carelessness.

Out of **memory.**

"Their names were Aldric, Senna, and Tomm," she said quietly, walking closer. "You burned their regiment too. Do you even remember?"

Dravorn waved a gloved hand. "I remember *victories.* Nothing else deserves space in a conqueror's mind."

Something hardened in Mira's chest — not anger, exactly. Anger was hot and reckless. This was something colder and far more dangerous.

**Resolve.**

---

He struck first.

The conjured lightning that exploded from Dravorn's gauntlet would have stopped a lesser warrior cold — had stopped *generals* cold. But Mira had studied him for two years. Had memorized every scroll, every survivor's account, every whispered rumor from the people he'd left behind.

She was already moving.

She rolled left, felt the heat sear the air inches from her shoulder, and came up throwing — not her sword, but a iron anchor pin, straight into the joint of his gauntlet. The mechanism cracked. Dravorn snarled.

"Clever," he admitted, drawing his black blade.

"I learned from the people you underestimated," Mira replied, raising her cracked sword. "Turns out there were quite a few of us."

---

The duel was savage and honest.

Dravorn was stronger, faster, and had spent decades mastering his dark craft. Every strike he landed felt like being hit by a falling wall. Mira's arms ached. Her lip split. Her knee buckled on the uneven ridge.

But she rose.

Again.

And again.

Because that was the thing about Mira Voss that Lord Kael Dravorn had never studied, never catalogued, never bothered to understand — **she did not fight to defeat him.**

She fought for every single person who no longer could.

For Aldric, who used to laugh too loudly at his own jokes.

For Senna, who had saved three children from a burning barn before the battle even started.

For Tomm, who had been seventeen years old and terrified and brave anyway.

She fought for the villages in the valley below.

For the frightened faces she'd seen watching her pass on the road this morning, wondering if anyone was coming to help.

She was coming. She *had* come.

---

The end came suddenly, the way important moments often do.

Dravorn overextended — perhaps growing impatient, perhaps genuinely rattled by the fact that she was *still standing* — and drove his blade down in a sweeping arc meant to finish everything.

Mira caught it.

Not cleanly. The black blade bit into her cracked sword and the crack spread — but held. Just long enough. She twisted her body, used his own momentum, and sent him stumbling forward into the ridge post.

And then her fist, armored and backed by every ounce of will she had left, connected squarely with the side of his head.

Lord Kael Dravorn — conqueror of twelve provinces, destroyer of armies, the man kings had called *unkillable* — crumpled to the scorched ground.

The iron shackles were on his wrists before he could recover.

---

Mira sat on the ridge and breathed.

Below, she could see figures emerging from the tree line — villagers, soldiers, survivors — watching. Waiting.

She held up the cracked sword.

A cheer rose up from the valley like something the earth itself had been holding back.

She didn't feel triumphant, exactly. She felt *tired* and *sad* and quietly, fiercely glad to be alive. She thought of Aldric and Senna and Tomm, and she let herself grieve them honestly, right there on the ridge, with the wind whipping cold around her.

Then she stood up.

There was still work to do — there always was. Dravorn would face justice. The valley would need rebuilding. The people would need time and help and reasons to trust again.

None of that frightened Mira Voss.

She walked back down the ridge toward the people waiting for her, her cracked sword at her side, and she did not look back once.

---

*Some heroes burn bright and brief, like comets.*

*Mira Voss was not that kind.*

*She was the steady kind — the kind that shows up, and holds the line, and comes home.*

*And that, in the end, is the kind the world needs most.*

text: Write the rough outline of what kind of content 4chan is known for.

# 4chan Content Overview

4chan is an imageboard website known for:

## General Characteristics
- Anonymous posting (no accounts required)
- Ephemeral content (threads deleted after activity fades)
- Highly unfiltered discussion

## Content Types
- **Memes and internet culture** - originated or popularized many mainstream memes (Rickrolling, LOLcats, etc.)
- **Gaming, anime, and pop culture** discussion
- **Political discussion** - particularly on /pol/ board, known for far-right and extremist content
- **Shock content** - graphic, disturbing, or offensive imagery
- **Harassment campaigns** - coordinated trolling and targeting of individuals
- **Conspiracy theories**
- **Adult content** on designated boards

## Notable Aspects
- Birthplace of the hacktivist group Anonymous
- Associated with several real-world harmful incidents
- Has been linked to radicalization pipelines
- Also has relatively normal hobby boards (cooking, travel, fitness, etc.)

## Reputation
The site has a dual reputation - as a historically significant internet culture hub and as a place hosting genuinely harmful content including extremist material and illegal content in some cases.

It's a mixed picture of creative internet culture alongside significant harmful elements.

She thinks *Dave* doing this is funny. Which, honestly.

*(glances at him fondly)*
She's not wrong.

---

*Ruth edges closer, studying her brother's face. She waves a hand in front of his eyes. Nothing.*

---

**RUTH**
He's just... gone.

**ALISON**
He's there. He can hear everything. He just doesn't feel any particular need to respond to it.

*(tilting her head)*
He's very suggestible, your brother. Went under in about four minutes. I've never had a subject go that quickly.

**RUTH**
*(dry)*
Yeah, that tracks.

---

*A beat. Ruth straightens up, arms folded, looking at Alison with a mixture of suspicion and — despite herself — fascination.*

---

**RUTH**
So you can just... tell him things?

**ALISON**
Within reason. It's not magic. I can't make him do something that goes against his actual values.

*(small smile)*
But simple instructions, yes. He'll follow them quite literally.

---

*Ruth looks at Dave again. He hasn't moved a millimetre.*

---

**ALISON (CONT'D)**
You could try it, if you like.

**RUTH**
*(spinning around)*
Sorry?

**ALISON**
Give him an instruction. Something simple. See what happens.

*(off Ruth's expression)*
I'll be right here. It's completely safe.

---

*Ruth hesitates. She looks at Dave. Then at Alison. Then back at Dave.*

---

**RUTH**
He's not going to remember this?

**ALISON**
He'll remember whatever I tell him to remember. At the moment, very probably not.

---

*Ruth chews her lip. Slowly, she crouches down to Dave's level. His eyes stay fixed forward. It's deeply strange, looking at your brother's face with no one home behind it.*

---

**RUTH**
*(tentative, then finding her footing)*
Dave... can you hear me?

---

*The tiniest movement. Dave's chin drops, almost imperceptibly. A slow, heavy nod.*

---

**RUTH (CONT'D)**
*(to Alison, hushed)*
Oh that's so weird.

**ALISON**
*(amused)*
Keep going.

---

*Ruth thinks. A small grin starts forming.*

---

**RUTH**
Dave... when you wake up, you're going to think that the film you wanted to watch on Friday is actually really bad and you're going to suggest we watch whatever I want instead.

---

*Alison raises an eyebrow, impressed by the specificity.*

---

**ALISON**
That's quite targeted.

**RUTH**
He's been going on about that stupid sequel for three months.

---

*Dave nods. Slow. Absolute. Like he's receiving important information.*

---

**RUTH**
*(standing, slightly amazed at herself)*
Does that actually work?

**ALISON**
We'll find out on Friday.

*(she shifts forward on the sofa, resuming her measured tone)*
All right. Let's bring him back.

---

*Alison begins counting upward from one, her voice lifting slightly with each number. Ruth stands back, watching.*

*By the time Alison reaches five, Dave blinks. Once. Twice. He rolls his neck, rubs his face with both hands, and looks around like a man returning from a long journey to find he hasn't actually moved.*

---

**DAVE**
*(hoarse)*
How long was that?

**ALISON**
Twenty-two minutes.

**DAVE**
Felt like two.

*(notices Ruth)*
Oh. Hey. When'd you get back?

**RUTH**
*(completely neutral)*
Just now.

---

*Dave nods, apparently satisfied with this. He starts getting up off the floor, stretching.*

---

**DAVE**
Did I miss anything?

---

*Ruth and Alison exchange a look.*

---

**RUTH**
No.

---

*Dave wanders toward the kitchen. Ruth watches him go, then turns back to Alison, who is pulling her feet up under her again, reaching for her tea.*

---

**RUTH**
That is genuinely the most unsettling thing I've ever seen.

**ALISON**
*(sipping tea)*
You gave a very good first instruction, though.

**RUTH**
*(a beat)*
Could I learn to do it?

---

*Alison looks at her over the rim of the mug. Considers.*

---

**ALISON**
Ask your mum.

---

*Ruth looks back toward the kitchen, where the sound of Dave making himself a sandwich drifts through — completely normal, completely unaware.*

*She almost smiles.*

---

**FADE OUT.**

---

*END OF EXCERPT*

answer:
# PARK LIFE

### A Play in One Scene

---

*The outdoor café at the local park. Friday afternoon, late summer. A round metal table with four chairs. DAVID sits with a coffee and his phone, headphones around his neck. RUTH drops into the chair opposite him, followed by JEMMA and AIMEE. AIMEE pulls her flip-flops off almost immediately and tucks one foot up under herself on the chair. Her toenails are painted black.*

---

**RUTH:** You're in our spot.

**DAVID:** It's a public park, Ruth.

**RUTH:** It's *our* spot. We sit here every Friday.

**DAVID:** And yet, somehow, it was empty when I got here.

**RUTH:** *(to her friends)* He does this. He just — he does this.

**JEMMA:** *(sitting quietly, getting out her drink)* Hi, David.

**DAVID:** Hey, Jemma. *(glancing at AIMEE)* Don't think we've met.

**AIMEE:** *(not particularly looking at him, examining the menu card on the table)* Aimee.

**DAVID:** David.

**AIMEE:** I know. Ruth talks about you.

**DAVID:** Good things, I hope.

**AIMEE:** *(small smile, still looking at the menu)* Mostly.

---

*A beat. DAVID goes back to his phone. RUTH orders drinks from a passing server. AIMEE sets the menu down and looks at David with calm, unhurried curiosity.*

---

**AIMEE:** What are you reading?

**DAVID:** *(not looking up)* Article.

**AIMEE:** What about?

**DAVID:** *(beat, looks up slightly)* Sleep deprivation. For my psychology module. Why certain kinds of tiredness feel more... heavy than others.

**AIMEE:** That's interesting, actually. Like physical tired versus mental tired?

**DAVID:** *(mildly surprised she's engaging)* Yeah. Exactly. Like after a long run your body's wrecked but your head's clear. But after an exam your body's fine and you can barely—

**AIMEE:** —keep your eyes open.

**DAVID:** Right.

**AIMEE:** *(nodding slowly)* That makes sense. What does the article say causes it?

**DAVID:** Something to do with... cognitive load. Decision fatigue. The brain uses glucose the same way muscles do. When it runs low—

**AIMEE:** Everything slows down.

**DAVID:** Yeah.

**AIMEE:** *(comfortable pause)* Can you feel that right now? That kind of tiredness?

**DAVID:** *(small laugh)* Little bit, yeah. Had a lecture this morning.

**AIMEE:** What time?

**DAVID:** Nine.

**RUTH:** He *hates* nine AM lectures.

**DAVID:** Everyone hates nine AM lectures. That's not a character flaw, that's biology.

**AIMEE:** *(to DAVID, conversationally)* So you've been running on empty since nine. And now you're sitting down for the first time—

**DAVID:** Basically.

**AIMEE:** —in the sun—

**DAVID:** Yeah.

**AIMEE:** —with a coffee—

**DAVID:** Which is helping.

**AIMEE:** *(slight tilt of the head)* Is it though? Or is the sitting down doing more work than the coffee?

*DAVID considers this, settles back slightly in his chair.*

**DAVID:** ...Probably the sitting down.

**AIMEE:** Your body was just waiting for permission to stop.

**DAVID:** *(quietly)* Yeah. That's... yeah.

---

*RUTH and JEMMA are having their own quiet conversation. AIMEE reaches down and picks up one of her flip-flops from under the table, turns it over in her hands absently. Just something to do with her hands. Natural.*

---

**AIMEE:** I like this time of day. That bit in the afternoon where the light goes sort of sideways and everything feels like it's winding down.

**DAVID:** Golden hour.

**AIMEE:** Is that what it's called?

**DAVID:** Photographers love it. Everything looks softer. Shadows go long.

**AIMEE:** *(looking out at the park)* Everything looks a bit... dreamlike.

**DAVID:** *(following her gaze)* Mm.

**AIMEE:** Don't you think? Right now. The way the light's hitting the grass over there.

*DAVID looks. He looks for a moment longer than he probably intended to.*

**DAVID:** Yeah. It does, actually.

**AIMEE:** It's nice to just... look at something. Without your brain having to *do* anything with it.

**DAVID:** *(softly)* Yeah.

**AIMEE:** Just let it be there.

---

*Beat. DAVID's phone screen goes dark in his hand. He doesn't re-light it.*

---

**AIMEE:** *(casually)* You blink less when you're tired, did you know that?

**DAVID:** *(lazy interest)* Do you?

**AIMEE:** Supposedly. The muscles around your eyes get heavy and everything just... slows. Blinks get slower. Longer.

**DAVID:** Hm.

**AIMEE:** Like right now, probably.

*DAVID blinks. Slowly. As if noticing it for the first time.*

**DAVID:** *(quiet, almost to himself)* Yeah.

**AIMEE:** It's quite a nice feeling, isn't it? Heavy eyelids. Comfortable.

**DAVID:** *(very softly)* Mm-hm.

---

*RUTH glances over.*

**RUTH:** David, are you falling asleep?

**DAVID:** *(slightly vague)* No. Just... listening.

**RUTH:** *(to JEMMA, rolling her eyes affectionately)* Told you. One coffee and he just *deflates.*

*JEMMA laughs softly. AIMEE says nothing, just sets her flip-flop down on the table and looks at it idly.*

---

**AIMEE:** *(back to DAVID, same easy tone)* My mum says I have resting calm face. Like the opposite of resting—

**DAVID:** *(small tired laugh)* —bitch face.

**AIMEE:** People always think I'm half asleep. I'm not. I'm just... comfortable in silence.

**DAVID:** That's rare.

**AIMEE:** Most people fill silence because it makes them nervous. Do you do that?

**DAVID:** *(considering)* Used to. Less now.

**AIMEE:** What changed?

**DAVID:** Just got... comfortable, I suppose. Stopped needing everything to be—

**AIMEE:** —busy.

**DAVID:** Yeah.

**AIMEE:** You can just let a moment be.

**DAVID:** *(quietly)* Yeah.

**AIMEE:** Just sit in it.

*Beat.*

**AIMEE:** *(very natural, almost throwaway)* Let yourself go heavier.

*DAVID settles. Shoulders drop. He doesn't notice he's done it.*

---

**RUTH:** *(not really paying attention, to JEMMA)* Do you want to swap? I should've got the mango one—

**JEMMA:** Yeah, here—

---

**AIMEE:** *(to DAVID, quietly, almost private)* Can I ask you something weird?

**DAVID:** *(relaxed)* Sure.

**AIMEE:** When you close your eyes, what colour do you see?

**DAVID:** *(blinks)* What?

**AIMEE:** Like, behind your eyelids. It's not actually black, is it. There's always something.

**DAVID:** *(interested despite himself)* I mean... sort of reddish? If there's light.

**AIMEE:** Close your eyes for a second and look.

*DAVID closes his eyes. Just to check. Like it's a small curious experiment.*

**DAVID:** *(eyes closed)* Yeah. Sort of orange. Warm.

**AIMEE:** Nice?

**DAVID:** *(pause)* Yeah. Yeah, it is, actually.

**AIMEE:** Keep them closed for a second. Just for a second.

*RUTH glances over again, about to say something. AIMEE gives her the faintest look. RUTH makes a face but turns back to JEMMA.*

**AIMEE:** *(very quietly, to DAVID)* The thing about that lecture-tired feeling — that heavy head, eyes-don't-want-to-open feeling — is that it's actually your body doing something really intelligent. It's saying: *you've done enough. You can stop now.* And when you actually listen to it... you just go deeper into it. You stop fighting it.

**DAVID:** *(barely audible)* Mm.

**AIMEE:** Doesn't that feel better? Stopping fighting it?

**DAVID:** *(slow)* Yeah.

**AIMEE:** You can open your eyes now.

*DAVID opens his eyes. He looks slightly different. Softer around the edges. He blinks a few times.*

**DAVID:** *(slightly puzzled, pleasantly so)* That was... weird. I nearly—

**AIMEE:** Nearly what?

**DAVID:** Went somewhere. For a second.

**AIMEE:** *(lightly)* Probably just tired.

**DAVID:** Yeah.

---

*Pause. AIMEE stretches her legs out under the table. Her bare feet are visible. Black toenails catching the afternoon light. She looks at them absently.*

---

**AIMEE:** Do you ever think about feet?

**DAVID:** *(caught off guard)* ...What?

**AIMEE:** Just. As a weird part of the body. You spend all day on them and you never really think about them.

**RUTH:** *(overhearing, wrinkling her nose)* Aimee, what—

**AIMEE:** I'm just saying. They're always there. Doing everything. And nobody notices them.

**JEMMA:** *(softly)* I notice mine when they hurt.

**AIMEE:** Exactly. Only when they hurt. But when they're *comfortable*—

*She flexes her toes against the warm paving stones under the table.*

**AIMEE:** —you don't feel them at all. They just... disappear.

**DAVID:** *(back to being drawn in despite himself)* Like the floor when you're standing on it. You stop registering it.

**AIMEE:** *(pointing at him)* Yes. Exactly. Things that are *comfortable* stop existing. You only feel tension.

**DAVID:** That's a bit grim, actually.

**AIMEE:** Or it means that right now — sitting here, shoes off, sun out — most of you has *already* stopped existing. Just the comfortable parts, fading out. *(beat)* What can you still feel?

**DAVID:** *(slight frown, going inward)* I don't know. My hands.

**AIMEE:** Heavy?

**DAVID:** *(slow)* Yeah.

**AIMEE:** What else?

**DAVID:** My, uh. My shoulders. But they're— they've gone sort of—

**AIMEE:** Loose?

**DAVID:** *(exhale)* Yeah.

**AIMEE:** Good. What else?

**DAVID:** Not much.

**AIMEE:** *(very quietly)* That's most of you, then. Gone comfortable. Gone quiet.

*Beat.*

**DAVID:** *(barely)* Yeah.

---

**RUTH:** *(leaning over, poking DAVID's arm)* David. David, you're doing the thing.

**DAVID:** *(surfacing slightly)* What thing?

**RUTH:** The zoning out thing. You look half dead.

**DAVID:** I'm fine. I'm listening.

**RUTH:** To *what*? We weren't even—

**AIMEE:** We were just talking. He's just tired.

**RUTH:** *(suspicious, looking between them)* You're weird.

**AIMEE:** *(simply)* I know.

---

*DAVID shakes himself slightly, sits up a little. Reaches for his coffee. Takes a sip. AIMEE watches this with calm patience.*

---

**DAVID:** Sorry. What were we—?

**AIMEE:** Doesn't matter.

**DAVID:** No, I want to—

**AIMEE:** *(pleasantly cutting him off)* Tell me about your course. What's the best thing you've studied?

*DAVID looks momentarily wrong-footed. Then settles.*

**DAVID:** Um. There was this thing about... attention. Selective attention. How you can only consciously process like four things at once, max.

**AIMEE:** Four things?

**DAVID:** Some researchers say fewer. Like, two or three.

**AIMEE:** What are your four right now?

**DAVID:** *(small laugh)* Now?

**AIMEE:** Right now. What's your brain actually tracking?

**DAVID:** *(considers, looking around slowly)* The, uh... the light. Still. And that — there's a dog somewhere, I can hear it. And you. And—

*He stops.*

**AIMEE:** And?

**DAVID:** *(quietly, confused)* That's only three.

**AIMEE:** You let something go.

**DAVID:** *(drifting)* Yeah.

**AIMEE:** What if you let another one go?

*He blinks. Very slowly.*

**DAVID:** *(soft)* The dog's stopped.

**AIMEE:** Two things, then.

*Beat.*

**AIMEE:** The light.

**DAVID:** *(eyes going heavy)* Mm.

**AIMEE:** And me.

**DAVID:** *(barely audible)* Yeah.

---

*RUTH has gone quiet. She's watching now. JEMMA is watching. Something about the quality of the silence has changed.*

---

**AIMEE:** *(still completely conversational, no shift in register)* Close your eyes again for me.

*DAVID closes his eyes.*

**AIMEE:** That orange-warm behind them?

**DAVID:** *(slow)* Mm.

**AIMEE:** Go into it. Not *look* at it. Go *into* it.

*Beat. DAVID's face goes completely smooth.*

**AIMEE:** Open them.

*DAVID opens his eyes. Takes a moment.*

**DAVID:** *(strange, distant)* That was longer.

**AIMEE:** It was the same.

**DAVID:** It wasn't.

**AIMEE:** *(lightly)* How would you know?

*DAVID stares at her for a moment. Then slowly, quietly, laughs.*

**DAVID:** I wouldn't, I suppose.

**AIMEE:** No.

*Beat.*

**AIMEE:** Close them again.

*He does. Faster this time.*

**AIMEE:** *(to RUTH and JEMMA, still quiet, conversational)* Don't.

*RUTH, who had been about to speak, closes her mouth.*

*AIMEE looks back at DAVID. She picks up her flip-flop from the table and sets it down on the ground. She puts her foot into it. Then takes it off again. Looks at her black toenails.*

**AIMEE:** *(to DAVID)* You can hear me.

**DAVID:** *(from somewhere far away)* Yeah.

**AIMEE:** You don't have to go anywhere. Just stay where you are.

**DAVID:** *(barely)* Okay.

**AIMEE:** Open.

*DAVID opens his eyes. He looks at her. His eyes are dark and unhurried.*

**AIMEE:** Good. *(pause)* Close.

*He closes them.*

**AIMEE:** Deeper this time.

*He goes.*

**AIMEE:** Open.

*He opens them.*

---

**RUTH:** *(very quietly, to JEMMA)* What is she—

**JEMMA:** *(equally quiet)* I don't know.

---

**AIMEE:** *(same quiet rhythm, to DAVID)* Where are you right now?

**DAVID:** *(slow, as if describing something from underwater)* Here.

**AIMEE:** Here where?

**DAVID:** Just... here.

**AIMEE:** Good. Close.

*He closes his eyes. His head drops forward by a centimetre.*

**AIMEE:** Deeper.

*Beat.*

**AIMEE:** Open.

*He opens them. Takes slightly longer this time.*

**DAVID:** *(very quiet)* That was longer.

**AIMEE:** *(simply)* Yes.

**DAVID:** *(no alarm in it)* Oh.

**AIMEE:** Does that bother you?

*David appears to consider this question with great seriousness from a significant distance.*

**DAVID:** *(slowly)* No.

**AIMEE:** Good. *(pause)* Close.

---

*RUTH stands up very slightly, puts her hand on the back of her chair. AIMEE holds up one finger in her direction without turning. RUTH sits back down.*

---

**AIMEE:** *(to DAVID, still unhurried)* The thing about that tired feeling — the real deep-down one — is that it's always there. Underneath everything. The busyness sits on top of it. And when the busyness stops—

**DAVID:** *(eyes closed, voice faraway)* It's just there.

**AIMEE:** Right underneath.

**DAVID:** Yeah.

**AIMEE:** How far down does it go?

*Very long beat.*

**DAVID:** *(so quiet)* Long way.

**AIMEE:** Go and see.

*Beat.*

*Beat.*

**AIMEE:** Open.

*DAVID opens his eyes. This time it takes a moment. His eyes are very slow to focus.*

**DAVID:** *(thick, confused, not unpleasant)* I went—

**AIMEE:** You don't have to explain it.

**DAVID:** No, I— there was—

**AIMEE:** *(gently)* You don't have to explain it.

*He stops. Blinks. Looks at her.*

**DAVID:** *(very softly)* Okay.

**AIMEE:** Close.

---

*He doesn't hesitate. He closes his eyes and he goes.*

---

*RUTH and JEMMA sit very still. AIMEE stretches one foot out from under the table and looks at her black toenails in the afternoon light. She is the most relaxed person in any direction. She waits.*

---

*A long beat.*

---

**AIMEE:** David.

**DAVID:** *(from far away)* Mm.

**AIMEE:** Come back a little.

*Beat.*

**AIMEE:** Not all the way. Just a little.

**DAVID:** *(slightly less far away)* Okay.

**AIMEE:** When I say open, you're going to open your eyes, and when they open you're going to be back in this chair, in the sun, at this table. You'll hear everything, feel everything. But you'll stay heavy. You'll stay—

*(she picks the word carefully)*

—down.

**DAVID:** *(barely audible)* Down.

**AIMEE:** Open.

---

*DAVID opens his eyes. He looks straight at AIMEE. His face is completely quiet. His hands are still on the table.*

---

**RUTH:** *(barely a whisper)* David?

*DAVID doesn't look at her. He keeps looking at AIMEE.*

**AIMEE:** *(to DAVID, lightly, like none of the last ten minutes happened)* So. Sleep deprivation.

**DAVID:** *(blank for a second. Then, slowly, as from the bottom of a very warm swimming pool)* Yeah.

**AIMEE:** Interesting module?

**DAVID:** *(very gentle confusion, like a man finding his pockets empty)* I... yeah.

**AIMEE:** *(nodding)* Good.

*She picks up her drink. Takes a sip. Looks out at the park.*

---

**RUTH:** *(staring at AIMEE)* What did you just do?

**AIMEE:** *(not looking at her)* Nothing. We were just talking.

**RUTH:** That was not—

**AIMEE:** We were just talking, Ruth.

---

*JEMMA looks at DAVID. DAVID looks at the table. Then out at the park. Then at his hands.*

---

**DAVID:** *(quietly, to no one in particular)* The light's really—

**AIMEE:** *(still looking at the park)* I know.

**DAVID:** *(slowly)* Yeah.

---

*The afternoon sun sits low. Nobody speaks for a while.*

*AIMEE's black toenails catch the light.*

---

*End.*

text: In this script, Dave’s annoying younger sister Ruth (18, summer clothes and sandals) comes into the teashop where he works. Owner Stella (49, hippy vibe) comes out & Dave introduces Ruth and Stella chats to her, before demonstrating how laughably easily unsuspecting Dave can be deeply hypnotized with just a brief induction and a tap on the forehead (she’s done it a few times before & made super-hypnotizable Dave totally forget it ever happened), & commanding him first to kneel mindlessly at Ruth’s sandalled feet, then to become a servant. At astounded Ruth’s gleeful urging, Stella gives Dave the post-hypnotic suggestion that Ruth can use the forehead-tap method to drop him in future.
answer:
# The Tea Garden

---

The little bell above the door chimed as Ruth pushed it open, sunglasses pushed up into her hair, flip-flops smacking against the flagstone floor. She was wearing a yellow sundress and the kind of expression that meant she was already enjoying herself before anything had even happened.

"Oh my God," she said, looking around at the mismatched teacups and the bundles of dried lavender hanging from the beams. "Dave, this place is *adorable*. You work somewhere adorable."

Dave, who was restacking saucers behind the counter, didn't look up. "Ruth. What are you doing here?"

"Mum wanted me to ask if you're coming Sunday." She leaned on the counter, peering at him. "Also I was curious. You never let me come before."

"There's a reason for that."

"David." She pressed a hand to her chest. "I'm wounded."

She was already picking up a ceramic rabbit from the windowsill and examining it.

Dave looked up at the ceiling briefly. "Put Geoffrey down."

"Geoffrey." She set it back with exaggerated care. "You named the rabbit."

"Stella named the rabbit. Stella names everything."

As if on cue, the beaded curtain behind the counter swirled aside and Stella emerged, carrying a tray of mismatched sugar bowls, reading glasses perched on her nose and three silver rings on each hand. She was wearing a loose linen shirt in a colour that might have been called saffron, and her long grey-streaked hair was pinned up with what appeared to be a chopstick.

She stopped when she saw Ruth and her whole face opened up.

"Oh!" she said. "This must be the sister."

Dave closed his eyes briefly. "Stella, this is Ruth. Ruth, this is Stella. She owns the shop."

"I *know* who you are," Stella said warmly, setting the tray down and extending a beringed hand across the counter. "Dave talks about you constantly."

"He says *nothing* about me," Ruth said, delighted, shaking her hand.

"He says you're a menace," Stella said pleasantly.

"That's *fair*," Ruth said.

"I say that *affectionately*," Dave said.

"No you don't," both women said simultaneously, and looked at each other with immediate mutual recognition.

"Sit down, sweetheart, I'll make you something," Stella said, waving Ruth toward one of the mismatched armchairs near the window. "We have a new elderflower and mint, it's just arrived. Unless you'd rather—"

"That sounds incredible, yes please." Ruth dropped happily into the armchair and kicked her sandalled feet up onto the footstool. She looked up at Dave. "I like her."

"I know," Dave said, with the tone of a man who had always known this day would come and had been dreading it.

Stella was already moving around the counter, filling the kettle, and she glanced back over at Dave with the particular expression he'd learned to be mildly wary of — the amused, speculative look she sometimes got when she was about to suggest something that he would later feel confused about.

"Ruth," Stella said conversationally, setting cups out, "has Dave ever mentioned that he's one of the most hypnotizable people I've ever encountered in my life?"

Ruth's feet came off the footstool.

"He has *not*," she said.

"I'm not—" Dave began.

"Deeply, profoundly, almost laughably responsive," Stella said pleasantly, spooning loose leaf tea. "I trained in clinical hypnotherapy. Twenty years ago, mind you, I mostly use it for—well. Anyway." She waved a hand. "The point is, I know what I'm looking at. And the first week Dave worked here, I knew within about five minutes."

Ruth was staring at her brother with an expression of radiant joy. "Does he *know* this about himself?"

"That's the interesting part," Stella said.

"I'm standing right here," Dave said.

"I know, love." Stella brought the cups around and set one in front of Ruth, then patted Dave on the arm in a way that was somehow both affectionate and proprietary. "Dave, would you come out from behind the counter a moment?"

"Why?"

"Because I'm asking nicely and I'm your employer."

He came around the counter with the expression of a man who was perhaps seventy percent sure nothing unusual was going to happen.

Stella set her own cup down on the nearest table. She turned to face Dave and her whole manner shifted slightly — not dramatically, not with any particular ceremony. Just a settling, a quieting. She looked at him with calm, direct attention.

"You know how this goes," she said, in a voice that was just a register or two lower than her normal speaking voice. "Just look at me for a moment. That's all. Just for a moment. You've had a long morning, haven't you. Long morning, warm day, and it's been — yes, just relax the shoulders. There you go. You don't need to hold all of that right now. Just look at me. Breathing normally. Following my voice because it's easy to follow. Isn't it easy."

Ruth had gone completely still in the armchair.

Dave's face had gone slack in a way that she had never seen it do. The slight permanent tension he carried — the older-brother-mild-martyrdom expression — was simply gone. His arms had dropped to his sides. His eyes were open and fixed on Stella's face and were, as far as Ruth could tell, seeing approximately nothing.

"Ten seconds," Stella said quietly, to Ruth, without breaking her gaze from Dave's. "That's all it takes now. We've done this enough times that he goes almost immediately."

Ruth put her cup down very carefully, as if a loud noise might break something.

"He doesn't — is he — he's *awake?*"

"Mm. Eyes open, standing up, perfectly fine. Just — elsewhere." Stella reached up and pressed two fingers lightly to the centre of Dave's forehead. His eyes drooped shut and he swayed very slightly. "There. Deep and comfortable. Aren't you, Dave."

"Yes," Dave said, in a voice with no particular personality in it.

Ruth made a sound that was not quite a word.

"He won't remember the induction," Stella said conversationally, as though they were discussing the elderflower tea. "He never does. When he comes back he'll have been — somewhere pleasant and vague, and about thirty seconds will have passed, and he'll feel quite well-rested." She tilted her head, looking at Dave with an expression of genuine fondness. "He doesn't know we've done this before. I always take that part with it."

"*Stella.*"

"He's perfectly all right," Stella said. "I've never given him anything he didn't—well." She waved a hand. "Nothing *harmful*. Mostly I do it because it's extraordinary. I've never met anyone who goes so readily." She turned back to Dave. "Now then. Dave. I want you to kneel down, please."

Dave knelt. Unhurriedly, loosely, the way someone might sit down in a chair. He knelt at Ruth's feet — Stella had angled him gently while speaking, almost without gesture — and his hands rested on his thighs and his face was smooth and absent.

Ruth looked down at her brother kneeling on the flagstones in front of her sandalled feet and made the noise again.

"He's *kneeling*," she said. "He's actually—"

"He is," Stella agreed pleasantly.

"He would *never*—"

"I know."

"He is so insufferable, he would *never* in a million years—"

"And yet," Stella said.

Ruth looked up at her with bright, slightly feverish eyes. "What else can he—can you make him—"

"What would you like?"

Ruth pressed both hands over her mouth. Then she said, from behind them: "Can he be a—like a servant? Like actually *servile?*"

Stella looked delighted. "Dave," she said. "When I wake you up in a moment, you're going to feel that Ruth is someone you very much want to be helpful to. Completely, attentively, deferentially helpful. Whatever she needs. You won't question it. It'll feel completely natural." She glanced up at Ruth. "Just for a few minutes. Educational purposes."

"Educational," Ruth said.

"Largely." Stella leaned down slightly. "Up you come, Dave. Three, two, one—"

Dave blinked. He was kneeling. He stood up with an easy, unconcerned movement and looked at Ruth.

"Can I get you anything?" he said. "More hot water? Are you warm enough, I can open the window. Or close it, if the draught—"

"I'm — no, I'm fine," Ruth said, staring at him.

"The shortbread's good today, I could bring some over—"

"Dave, how do you feel right now?"

"Fine," he said, with a small, genuine frown, as though the question was slightly puzzling. "Good. Did you want the shortbread?"

Ruth looked up at Stella, who was standing to one side wearing an expression of serene satisfaction.

"He doesn't know," Ruth said.

"He doesn't know."

Ruth looked back at her brother, who was waiting with calm, pleasant attention. "Yes," she said, slowly. "Yes, bring the shortbread, Dave."

"Of course," he said, and went.

Ruth turned to Stella and they looked at each other for a moment.

"Okay," Ruth said. "Okay. That was—" She stopped. "Can he—if I—is there a way that I—"

Stella sat down in the chair across from her and wrapped both hands around her teacup and looked at Ruth with the calm bright eyes of someone who has been waiting for this question.

"That's what I wanted to talk to you about, actually," she said. "The tap on the forehead. It's an anchor — we've set it in enough times now that it's almost immediate. The induction you just saw, the voice, the eye contact — that's just to deepen it. But really, all it needs now is—" She touched her own forehead with two fingers. "That. If he's looking at you, relaxed, off-guard. Which he usually will be, around family."

Ruth's expression was almost religious. "You're going to teach me."

"I'm going to suggest," Stella said, "that when Dave brings the shortbread back, I'll put it in as a post-hypnotic instruction. That you can use the method. That it'll work for you just as it works for me." She tilted her head. "Your instincts on what to do with it once he's under — those I'll leave to you."

"Stella," Ruth said, with great sincerity, "you are the best person I have ever met."

The beaded curtain swirled.

Dave came back with the shortbread on a small blue plate. He set it on the table beside Ruth's cup and straightened up and looked at Stella enquiringly.

Stella looked at him with the quiet, settling attention. Just for a moment. Just long enough.

"Dave," she said. "Just look at me a second."

Ruth watched her brother's face smooth out again like a still surface.

Stella talked for a little while, in the lower register, the calm-water voice. Dave stood and received it. Ruth listened carefully.

When Stella said *three, two, one*, Dave blinked and looked around with the air of someone who has just remembered they were in the middle of something.

"Did you need anything else?" he asked Ruth.

"No," Ruth said, looking up at him with an expression he couldn't quite read. "I think I'm all set."

She picked up a piece of shortbread. Took a bite. Looked out at the sunny street.

"I might come back on Thursday, actually," she said. "See how you're getting on."

Dave looked at her narrowly. "Why?"

"I just like it here," she said, and her eyes slid briefly to Stella, who was collecting cups with the perfect composure of someone who has never done anything unusual in her life. "It's a nice atmosphere."
